items.label: f02-senior-ownership-checklist
items.front: What does a senior check, in order, to rule out IDOR in a CRUD codebase?
items.back: 1) Does the resource have an owner/tenant column? 2) Is every read filtered by it? 3) Does every write verify it before mutating? 4) Is the check centralized (global query filter / policy) or copy-pasted? 5) Do tests prove cross-user denial?

items.label: f08-interview-loop-leads
items.front: With one system-design or deep-dive interview slot, which ADR answers does the interview-translation guide say to lead with, and what should each one show?
items.back: ADR-003, ADR-009 or ADR-010. Each shows the junior-to-senior gradient in one breath: name the decision, what it costs, the failure mode, and the fix. The golden rule throughout: answer with a concrete example, a tradeoff and a failure mode, never a definition.

items.label: f10-openapi-build-input
items.front: Why does the API-design guide treat netcleanarch's OpenAPI document as a build input rather than documentation?
items.back: Both frontends generate their typed API clients from it with NSwag (see ClientApp-React/nswag.json). The API is not the last stop: its contract feeds the builds of two other codebases.

items.label: f07-problem-details-arms
items.front: Which HTTP status does ProblemDetailsExceptionHandler give a validation, a not-found, an unauthorized and a forbidden exception?
items.back: ValidationException: 400, with the field-errors dictionary as ValidationProblemDetails. NotFoundException (thrown by Guard.Against.NotFound): 404. UnauthorizedAccessException: 401. ForbiddenAccessException: 403. The last two are both thrown by AuthorizationBehaviour.

items.label: f03-cookie-vs-bearer
items.front: Cookie vs bearer auth: which attack each shifts onto you, and when each fits.
items.back: Cookie: HttpOnly so XSS cannot read it, but sent automatically so CSRF becomes your problem; fits an SPA served by the API. Bearer: sent explicitly so CSRF is mostly moot, but client storage makes XSS your problem; fits public APIs, cross-origin and mobile.

items.label: f01-two-auth-points
items.front: Name the two authorization enforcement points in netcleanarch and what each buys.
items.back: Endpoint groups with RequireAuthorization(): fail fast with a proper HTTP 401 challenge. [Authorize] on request records enforced by AuthorizationBehaviour: works without HTTP and survives new transports. Inconsistency: only GetTodosQuery carries [Authorize].

items.label: f05-four-test-seams
items.front: Name netcleanarch's four test projects, the seam each one enters at, and the real infrastructure each runs against.
items.back: Domain.UnitTests: plain objects, no infrastructure. Application.UnitTests: one class plus mocks, no infrastructure. Application.FunctionalTests: ISender, against a real database (Aspire + Respawn). Web.AcceptanceTests: a real browser (Playwright + Gherkin) over the full stack, SPA included.

items.label: f06-assert-mapping-config
items.front: What does the `AssertConfigurationIsValid()` test in MappingTests buy the team?
items.back: It turns 'we forgot to update the AutoMapper profile' from a runtime surprise into a build failure. One test, and the testing guide's author calls it their favorite in the repo.

items.label: f04-events-are-calls
items.front: Why does ADR-009 call these domain events 'synchronous method calls in disguise', and what delivery guarantee do they have?
items.back: Publish awaits all handlers inline, so their latency and failures land on the user's request. Delivery is at-most-once, in-process, and lost on crash.

items.label: f11-endpoint-group-convention
items.front: How does an IEndpointGroup class become a live route group, and which C# language feature does the interface rely on?
items.back: At startup MapEndpoints reflects over the assembly and registers each class implementing IEndpointGroup as a route group named /api/{ClassName}, with a matching OpenAPI tag. The interface declares a `static abstract Map`, which was impossible before C# 11.

items.label: f09-no-repository-layer
items.front: ADR-004: how do handlers reach EF Core, why is there no repository layer, and how does that tie into the testing strategy?
items.back: Application defines IApplicationDbContext (DbSet<TodoList>, DbSet<TodoItem>, SaveChangesAsync); ApplicationDbContext in Infrastructure implements it, and handlers use full LINQ against it. Repositories were rejected because they hide the EF coupling instead of removing it. The cost: handlers cannot be unit-tested against a mocked repository, so they need a real database, which is why ADR-008's testing strategy exists. The two decisions reinforce each other.

items.prompt: A fork writes `[Authorize(Roles = "Admin, User")]`, with a space after the comma. Per the error-handling guide, what happens to a signed-in user whose only role is `User`?

choices.text: Access granted, as each split entry is trimmed before it meets the user's roles
A 401, as a role that can never match is treated like having no signed-in user
A startup failure, as role strings with spaces are refused at app registration
A 403, as splitting without Trim leaves a role named " User" that never matches

choices: Access granted, as each split entry is trimmed before it meets the user's roles
A 401, as a role that can never match is treated like having no signed-in user
A startup failure, as role strings with spaces are refused at app registration
A 403, as splitting without Trim leaves a role named " User" that never matches

items.explanation: Line 38: the role check splits with `Split(',')` and no `Trim()`, so the second entry is a role literally named " User" that never matches. Line 36: UnauthorizedAccessException (401) is for no authenticated user at all, ForbiddenAccessException (403, line 11) for an authenticated user lacking the role, which is this user. The guide calls the edge latent because no caller passes such a string, so nothing rejects it at startup.

items.prompt: A developer renames the endpoint handler method `GetTodoLists` to `FetchAllTodoLists`. According to the API-design guide, why is that a breaking API change?

choices.text: The backend stops compiling, as a test project still calls the handler by its old name
The operationId comes from the method name, so both SPAs get a renamed client method
Only server log labels change, as no client depends on any handler method name
Nothing visible changes, as NSwag names client methods from the route and verb

choices: The backend stops compiling, as a test project still calls the handler by its old name
The operationId comes from the method name, so both SPAs get a renamed client method
Only server log labels change, as no client depends on any handler method name
Nothing visible changes, as NSwag names client methods from the route and verb

items.explanation: API design, Decision 1 (lines 15-19): the endpoint's name, which becomes the OpenAPI operationId, is derived from the handler method's name via `.WithName(handler.Method.Name)`, so the C# method GetTodoLists becomes the generated TypeScript method getTodoLists(). Renaming the method changes the operationId and therefore the generated client method in both SPAs, breaking every call site and any external OpenAPI consumer. In the incident (line 52) the backend CI stayed green because C# compiled fine; it was the frontend build that failed.

items.prompt: In the MediatR pipeline, AuthorizationBehaviour is registered before ValidationBehaviour. What does that ordering protect?

choices.text: Validation errors get logged together with the authenticated user's name
Anonymous callers never get validation feedback that could leak which resources exist
Performance timing then excludes the cost of the authorization database lookups
Validators can safely assume the request's IDs already belong to the caller

choices: Validation errors get logged together with the authenticated user's name
Anonymous callers never get validation feedback that could leak which resources exist
Performance timing then excludes the cost of the authorization database lookups
Validators can safely assume the request's IDs already belong to the caller

items.explanation: The ADR calls the order load-bearing: exception logging wraps authorization, authorization precedes validation, and performance timing is innermost so it measures only the handler.

Only see list titles, because the items are loaded through a per-user global filter
Nothing harmful, because RequireAuthorization scopes every query to the caller
Read or change other users' lists, because nothing records or checks an owner

It swallows every exception thrown by the domain event handlers
It blocks on async work, which deadlocks wherever a synchronization context exists
It dispatches each event twice, once per SaveChanges overload

It dispatches each event twice, once per SaveChanges overload

choices.text: Only once an event has more than one handler registered for it
Never: in-process dispatch already guarantees at-least-once delivery
As soon as the database provider moves from SQLite to SQL Server
As soon as a handler performs external I/O such as sending email

items.explanation: Today every handler only logs, so the ghost-notification risk is latent; the outbox is the standard answer for reliable external side effects.

400 ValidationProblemDetails, the same as any other invalid field
422, because the domain rejects the value after validation passes

items.prompt: Domain events are published by a SaveChanges interceptor before the commit. A handler sends an email, then the save fails. What happened?

choices.text: The save is retried until it succeeds, so the email becomes true
Nothing: the email is queued in the same transaction and rolled back
A ghost notification: the email left even though the change never committed
The interceptor publishes again after the retry, sending two emails

items.prompt: Two functional tests occasionally corrupt each other's data, and a colleague proposes marking them `[Parallelizable]` to shake out the flake. What does the testing guide say that would do, and what is the right first fix?

choices.text: It would cause the cross-talk, so first remove the static user fields in TestApp
It would be safe, as the static user fields are scoped to each test's own thread
It would cause the cross-talk, so first give each test its own database copy
It would speed things up safely, as Respawn already isolates each test's data

choices: It would cause the cross-talk, so first remove the static user fields in TestApp
It would be safe, as the static user fields are scoped to each test's own thread
It would cause the cross-talk, so first give each test its own database copy
It would speed things up safely, as Respawn already isolates each test's data

items.explanation: Lines 35-39: the test's current user is stored in static, process-global fields in TestApp, so two tests running at once would stomp on each other's identity, and Respawn's per-test reset assumes one test touches the database at a time; that is why the suite runs serially. Enabling parallelism would cause the very cross-talk the colleague imagines fixing, and the guide says the right fix is to remove the statics first.

External side effects such as emails are delivered exactly once
Handlers run on a background thread, off the user's HTTP request

items.prompt: A fork's dashboard fired 500-rate alerts because an API integration sent unsupported colour codes. What standing practice does the error-handling guide draw from that incident?

choices.text: Swap domain exceptions for Result objects so that none can escape a handler
Add a catch-all switch arm and report any unknown exception as a 400 instead
Route all API clients through the UI swatch picker so bad colours cannot arrive
Grep Domain and Application for every Exception subclass and confirm it is mapped

items.explanation: Line 50: every exception type that can escape a handler needs a deliberate HTTP identity, so periodically grep the Domain and Application layers for `: Exception` and check each one is mapped; an unmapped domain exception is a latent 500. Line 28 keeps unmapped-to-500 as the right default for genuinely unexpected exceptions such as a NullReferenceException; the guide treats the API, not the UI, as the contract, and keeps throwing for domain-contract violations.

items.prompt: A create request arrives with three invalid fields. What does the client get back, according to the error-handling guide?

choices.text: One 400 listing all three, gathered by the validation behaviour before one throw
One 400 naming the first failure, as validation halts at the first broken rule

items.explanation: Line 14: ValidationBehaviour, a MediatR pipeline stage, runs all validators for the request, aggregates all failures and throws a single ValidationException carrying a PropertyName to messages dictionary, so the client gets every problem with its input at once. The aggregation happens in the pipeline behaviour, not in the endpoint, and line 52 describes one-failure-per-round-trip as exactly what this design prevented.

items.prompt: A pull request adds a field to a command that clients must never be allowed to set. Per Decision 2 of the API-design guide, what should change?

items.explanation: Line 27: commands are the bind target, so a client could set a server-controlled field in the request body (mass-assignment / over-posting), which the guide calls a real vulnerability, not a theoretical one, with nothing structural stopping it. Its prescription is to ask of each new field whether the client should be allowed to set it and, if not, to give that endpoint a real request DTO; the direct-bind convention is kept everywhere else, and a validator rule is not what the guide prescribes.

The other reasons belong to other choices: the mocked or in-memory context was rejected for passing queries the real provider can't translate (line 15), container-per-test for being far slower (line 16), and the static current-user fields are why the suite cannot run in parallel (line 27).

items.explanation: Lines 38-40: the check is about the relationship between the URL and the payload, a transport-level HTTP idea the handler shouldn't need to know exists, so it stays in the endpoint. The tradeoff the author watches 'like a hawk' is growth: next a null check, then a 'quick' business rule, until endpoints hold logic the handlers don't know about and the tests don't cover. The guide classifies it as transport logic, not a business rule, and ties it to neither authentication nor resource-existence leaks.

items.explanation: Line 14: each layer's blind spot is another layer's target, and when you decide where a test goes the rule is to test at the lowest layer that can observe the failure you actually fear. Pushing a fear down a layer is faster but fictional; pushing it up is real but slow and vague. So the rule is neither 'highest' nor 'fastest', and it places a fear at one layer rather than at all of them.

items.explanation: Line 24: the codebase deliberately uses both. 'The password was too weak' is an expected outcome the caller branches on, so Identity returns a Result; domain-contract violations throw. The mature answer is that it depends on whether the failure is exceptional or expected. Line 22 says Result was rejected as the default, and the guide never chooses by where the code lives or by which status results.
